subject: Culture
title: Food Sovereignty
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Food Sovereignty.

hook.text: La Vía Campesina represents 200 million farmers who demand the right to grow their own food their own way.

buildup.text: Food sovereignty opposes corporate control of seeds, land, and farming methods.

discovery.text: Monsanto once sued farmers for saving seeds. Corporate patents turned ancient practices into crimes.

twist.text: Indigenous communities in the Andes still grow 4,000 potato varieties. Monoculture threatens that diversity.

climax.text: Who controls the food controls the future. Sovereignty starts at the seed.

quiz.question: What does the food sovereignty movement primarily oppose?

details.summary: Food sovereignty is the right of peoples to define their own food systems — what they grow, how they grow it, and who profits. This movement pushes back against corporate agriculture and international trade rules that prioritize profit over local food cultures and farmer autonomy.
details.whyItMatters: Food sovereignty challenges the global food system's power structures. It asks who controls what the world eats — local communities or multinational corporations.
takeaways: La Via Campesina coined 'food sovereignty' in 1996
The movement opposes corporate control of seed and food systems
Indigenous food sovereignty reclaims traditional agricultural practices

faq.question: What is food sovereignty?
faq.answer: Food sovereignty is the right of peoples to healthy and culturally appropriate food produced through ecologically sound methods, and their right to define their own food systems.

faq.question: How does food sovereignty differ from food security?
faq.answer: Food security means everyone has enough food — regardless of where it comes from. Food sovereignty adds the dimension of control — communities should determine what is grown, how it is grown, and who benefits.
